cards.explanation: The answer is the kings of Israel. Ahaz, king of Judah, “…walked in the ways of the kings of Israel…” instead of doing what was right in the LORD's eyes. Remember he comes from David's line, so he's wandering a long way from the family recipe. The text names Israel's kings and nobody else.

The answer is False. The text says Ahaz “…sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.” Those are the places the verse names, friends. The temple isn't one of them.

The answer is Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria. Verse 7 says Ahaz sent messengers to him. Judah's king is under attack, and Assyria is who he calls. I'd have phoned a different number, but that's the call he made.

The answer is that Ahaz calls himself your servant and your son. He tells the king of Assyria, “I am your servant and your son.” Then he asks him to come up and save him from the kings of Aram and Israel. A king calling himself somebody else's servant is a lot to say in one sentence.

The answer is silver and gold from the LORD's house and the palace. Ahaz took the silver and gold found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's palace. Then he sent it as a gift to the king of Assyria. Silver and gold from two places, friends, all in one gift.
The answer is True. The king of Assyria marched up to Damascus and captured it. He also put Rezin, king of Aram, to death. Rezin was one of the two kings who came against Ahaz, so that's a big turn.
The answer is False. The king of Assyria took the people of Damascus to Kir as captives. They didn't get to stay in their city. It's a hard part of the story, friends, and the text doesn't soften it.

The answer is that Uriah builds the altar by Ahaz's instructions. Uriah the priest builds the altar according to all the instructions King Ahaz sent from Damascus. He doesn't change a thing, as far as the text tells us. I once had a recipe card that I followed less closely than that.

The answer is True. Verse 11 says Uriah completed the altar before King Ahaz returned. So when the king gets back, the altar is already finished. The text puts the finish line before the king's return, and that's all it says about timing.

The answer is that Ahaz approaches the altar and presents offerings on it. When the king came back from Damascus and saw the altar, he approached it and presented offerings on it (verse 12). Verse 13 then lists what he offered, starting with his burnt offering and his grain offering.

The answer is that Ahaz moves it to the north side of the new altar. He took the bronze altar that stood before the LORD and put it on the north side of the new altar. It had been standing between the new altar and the house of the LORD. So the bronze altar ends up on the north side of the new one, friends.

The answer is the great new altar. Ahaz tells Uriah to offer the morning burnt offering, the evening grain offering and all the people's offerings on the great altar. He keeps the bronze altar for himself, to seek guidance. Uriah gets the daily work, and the king keeps the bronze altar.

The answer is False. Verse 16 says, “So Uriah the priest did just as King Ahaz had commanded.” There's no objection recorded anywhere, friends. The text moves straight from the king's orders to Uriah doing them.
The answer is True. Ahaz cut off the frames of the movable stands and removed the bronze basin from each of them. The text says it plainly. He's not tinkering, he's taking things apart.

The answer is Assyria. Verse 18 says Ahaz removed the Sabbath canopy and closed the royal entryway on account of the king of Assyria. That's the same king he sent silver and gold to earlier. The text gives the king of Assyria as the reason, and doesn't say more than that.

The answer is Hezekiah. Ahaz is buried with his fathers in the City of David, and his son Hezekiah reigns in his place. A new king takes the throne. This chapter leaves it right there, friends, so the story isn't over.
